newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria to avoid winter energy crisis - minister.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria to avoid winter energy crisis - minister.

text.p: Bulgarian Energy Minister Roumen Ovcharov said on Friday the country would have enough electricity supplies during the coming winter despite a chronic lack of funds for the energy sector.
In an interview with Reuters, Ovcharov said his ministry had done "everything in its abilities" to ensure normal electricity supplies.
The ministry has signed a contract with Russia for emergency power supplies.
But Ovcharov said a chronic shortage of cash would create problems very soon. "The problems will come up at the beginning of next year," he added.
The ministry has to pay huge amounts in the coming several months, including $22 million for already supplied Russian nuclear fuel and $6-7 million for coal deliveries.

At the beginning of 1997 Bulgaria must pay Russia another $30 million for fuel for reactors number two, four and five at the Soviet-designed 3,760-megawatt nuclear plant at Kozloduy, which supplies almost half of the country's electricity.
Ovcharov said $1.5 million would be spent on safety upgrading of Kozloduy's oldest reactor number one, which was switched off in May in response to international concern.
Samples of the vessel's metal of the 440-megawatt reactor will be studied by Russia's Korchatov Institute and preliminary results are expected in November.
Ovcharov said reconstruction of the reactor should be completed by December and if official results proved the metal was safe, the reactor would be restarted on February 1.
"If we do not receive money, the biggest project we will have to give up will be the country's structural reform," he said.
"What will happen to the planned privatisation? No one will come to invest in a country which lacks normal electricity supplies."

Ovcharov on Friday withdrew his proposal for a fresh energy price rise next month under pressure from local media and after Deputy Prime Minister Roumen Gechev opposed the ministry's energy pricing system.
"I want to have the clear support of the government...in this difficult (economic) situation...I do not wish to be seen as a lonely long distance runner," Ovcharov said.

Under the pricing mechanism, since July energy prices have been revised each month mainly according to the inflation rate and the lev/dollar exchange rate. But rising prices of electricity, coal and central heating are choking the economy and the overstretched budgets of ordinary Bulgarians. -- Sofia Newsroom, +359-2-84561
